candidate.derivedAnswer: A, the line segment from A to B, including both endpoints
candidate.answerReason: Segment addition gives equality on the segment. Triangle inequality excludes points off the line, and points beyond either endpoint give a strictly larger sum.

methods.label: Check points on and outside the segment
methods.explanation:
We need to show both that every point on the segment works and that every point outside it fails. First suppose \(A\ne B\).

If \(P\) lies on the segment from \(A\) to \(B\), segment addition gives \(AP+PB=AB\). This includes \(P=A\) and \(P=B\), since undirected distances may be zero.

If \(P\) is off the line through \(A\) and \(B\), the three points form a triangle. The triangle inequality gives \(AP+PB>AB\), so such a point fails.

If \(P\) is on the line but outside the segment, let \(d>0\) be its distance to the nearer endpoint. Its distance to the farther endpoint is \(AB+d\), so
\[
AP+PB=AB+2d>AB.
\]
These cases cover every point.

If \(A=B\), the condition becomes \(2AP=0\), so only \(P=A\) works, again the segment with endpoints \(A\) and \(B\). Therefore the required set is the entire line segment from \(A\) to \(B\), choice A.
methods.levelReason: Segment addition and the elementary triangle inequality establish the locus without coordinate algebra or conic sections.
